differentiate between organic and inorganic compounds;
differentiate between condensation (dehydration synthesis) and hydrolysis reactions;
describe properties of carbon, i.e., tetravalency, isomerism, and catenation;

subtopics.name: 1.3 The Significance of Water’s Chemical Nature in Supporting Life Processes

slos.description: describe the polarity of water molecules that results in hydrogen bonding;

discuss the properties of water that contribute to the sustainability of life on Earth, i.e.,
a. cohesion and adhesion,
b. high specific heat,
c. anomalous behaviour of water,
d. high heat of vapourisation,
e. hydrophobic exclusion,
f. ionisation of water;
define carbohydrates;
classify carbohydrates as monosaccharides, disaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides with examples;
compare the properties and roles of monosaccharides with their formulae;
distinguish between D and L forms of glucose (stereoisomers) based on the spatial arrangement of hydroxyl (-OH) groups around their chiral carbons;
illustrate the structure of α-D-glucose and β-D-glucose based on the position of the hydroxyl group at the anomeric carbon;

illustrate the condensation (dehydration synthesis) and hydrolysis (breakdown) of disaccharides (sucrose, lactose and maltose) and polysaccharides (amylose, amylopectin, cellulose, starch and glycogen) by formation and breakage of glycosidic bonds;
relate the structures of starch (amylose and amylopectin), glycogen and cellulose molecules to their functions in living organisms;
define lipids;
describe the properties of triglycerides (triacylglycerols), phospholipids, terpenoids (terpenes, carotenoids and steroids) and waxes with examples;
differentiate between saturated and unsaturated fatty acids;
illustrate the condensation and hydrolysis of a triglyceride molecule;
illustrate the molecular structure of triglycerides, phospholipids, terpenoids (terpenes, carotenoids and steroids) and waxes;
define proteins and amino acids;
illustrate the structure of amino acids;
explain that the amphoteric nature of amino acids enables them to function as buffers;
illustrate the condensation (dehydration synthesis) and hydrolysis (breakdown) of peptide linkages;

differentiate between:
a. essential and non-essential amino acids,
b. acidic and basic amino acids,
c. polar and non-polar amino acids;

describe the types of interaction that hold protein molecules in shape:
a. hydrophobic interactions,
b. hydrogen bonding,
c. ionic bonding,
d. covalent bonding (including disulfide bonds),
e. Van der Waals forces;
differentiate among levels of organisation of proteins, i.e., primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary with examples;
differentiate between fibrous and globular proteins with examples;
relate the structure of haemoglobin (globular protein) and collagen (fibrous protein) to their functions;
explain that change of amino acid sequence in a polypeptide chain leads to sickle cell anaemia;
describe the functions of proteins in living organisms;
define nucleic acid;
illustrate the basic structure of a nucleotide and a nucleoside;

analyse the structure of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) molecule as a double helix, including:
a. the importance of complementary base pairing between the 5′ to 3′ strand and the 3′ to 5′ strand (antiparallel strands),
b. differences in hydrogen bonding between C–G and A–T base pairs,
c. linking of nucleotides by phosphodiester bonds,
d. synthesis and breakdown of polynucleotides by the formation and breakage of phosphodiester bonds;
classify nucleotides based on their sugar molecules and nitrogen bases;
compare the structure and function of messenger RNA (mRNA), ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and transfer RNA (tRNA);
differentiate between DNA and RNA;
define conjugated molecules;
describe the functions of glycolipids, glycoproteins, lipoproteins and nucleoproteins with examples;
define structural biology;
explain the process of X-ray crystallography, including the generation of X-rays, crystal preparation, diffraction pattern collection and structure determination;
describe the contribution of Rosalind Franklin’s in the discovery of the DNA double helix structure particularly through her X-ray diffraction images;
define biological databases;
describe the purpose of biological databases;
state different primary biological databases [(e.g., GenBank, UniProt, Protein Data Bank (PDB), Protein Information Resource (PIR))].

describe the following terms:
a. enzyme,
b. apoenzyme,
c. holoenzyme,
d. active site,
e. allosteric site;
classify cofactors based on their characteristic features into prosthetic groups, essential ions or activators and coenzymes, with examples;
analyse the effects of absence or deficiency of specific cofactors on enzyme function including common examples (i.e., Fe²⁺, Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺ and B-complex vitamins);

analyse the mode of action of enzymes in terms of:
a. an active site,
b. enzyme–substrate complex,
c. lowering of activation energy,
d. enzyme specificity, with the help of lock-and-key and induced-fit hypotheses;
evaluate the effect of different factors, i.e., temperature, pH, substrate concentration, enzyme concentration on the rate of enzyme action;
analyse the effect of temperature on the rate of enzyme action in human body and thermophilic bacteria;
analyse the effect of pH on the activity of different enzymes, i.e., amylase, trypsin, pepsin, lipase and papain;
define enzyme inhibition;
differentiate between reversible and irreversible inhibitors with examples;
analyse the effects of reversible inhibitors, i.e., competitive and non-competitive on enzyme activity;
define end product inhibition (feedback inhibition);
explain the mechanism of end product inhibition;
describe the significance of inhibitors in regulation of enzymatic activity, medical applications and industrial processes such as preserving food;
classify enzymes based on their substrates, i.e., lipases, diastase, amylase and proteases with examples;
classify enzymes based on reactions they catalyse and nature of substrate, i.e., oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, isomerases and ligases with examples.
state classical cell theory;
describe exceptions to classical cell theory, i.e., status of virus and the first cell, which could not have arisen from a pre-existing cell;

describe the process of validating cell theory with historical and modern evidence, i.e., early microscopes provide initial evidence and modern techniques like electron microscopy and molecular biology further support it;
compare classical and modern cell theory;
state the contributions of different scientists in the discovery of cell (Robert Hooke 1665 to August Weismann 1880);
compare the resolution and magnification of light microscope and electron microscope (including transmission electron microscope and scanning microscope);
evaluate the suitability of different microscopy techniques based on their magnification and resolution capabilities for specific applications (e.g., viewing live cells vs. fixed tissues);
calculate magnification, image size and actual size of the specimen by using the formula: Magnification = Image size (viewed under microscope) ÷ Actual size;

subtopics.name: 3.3 Structure of Animal and Plant Cell

slos.description: describe that cells are the basic unit of life with respect to properties of life, i.e., movement, respiration, homeostasis, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition;

explain the structure, chemical composition and functions of the cellular organelles of eukaryotic cell as revealed through the electron microscope:
a. cell wall,
b. cell membrane with reference to Fluid Mosaic Model,
c. cytoplasm,
d. rough endoplasmic reticulum and smooth endoplasmic reticulum,
e. ribosomes,
f. mitochondria,
g. Golgi apparatus,
h. lysosomes,
i. vacuoles,
j. cytoskeleton (microfilaments, microtubules and intermediate filaments),
k. cilia and flagella,
l. centrioles,
m. plastids and its types,
n. nucleus,
o. peroxisomes,
p. glyoxisomes;
compare the structure of animal and plant cells;
assess that different organelles interact to maintain cellular functions, i.e., protein synthesis and transport;
analyse the effect of malfunctioning of a specific organelle on the overall function of cell;

describe the role of phospholipids, cholesterol, glycolipids, proteins and glycoproteins in cell surface membranes, with reference to stability, fluidity, permeability, transport proteins (e.g., carrier proteins and channel proteins), cell signalling (e.g., cell surface receptors) and cell recognition (e.g., cell surface antigens);
define the terms cell signalling and ligands;
explain the main stages of cell signalling, i.e., reception, transduction, transmission to effector and response;
compare mechanisms of passive transport (e.g., simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis) and active transport;

explain the factors influencing the rate of diffusion, i.e., concentration gradient, temperature, molecular size, medium of diffusion, surface area, distance, solvent density, permeability of the membrane, pressure and chemical nature of the molecule;

analyse the roles of active and passive transport mechanisms in the movement of substances across cell membranes and their impact on homeostasis, nutrient uptake, waste removal and overall cell survival;
explain the steps involved in endocytosis and exocytosis, i.e., vesicle formation, movement and membrane fusion;
explain the types of endocytosis, i.e., phagocytosis and pinocytosis;
elaborate the significance of endocytosis and exocytosis in maintaining cellular function;
describe storage diseases with reference to the malfunctioning of lysosomes, i.e., Tay-Sachs disease, Gaucher’s disease, Krabbe’s disease, glycogenosis type-II disease;
state the characteristic features of stem cells;
explain different types of stem cells based on their potency, i.e., totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent;
describe the advantages and disadvantages of using induced pluripotent stem cells.
describe the basis of classification of living organisms, i.e., homology, biochemistry, cytology and genetics;
describe the hierarchical structure of biological classification including domain, kingdom, phylum/ division, class, order, family, genus and species;
describe the principles of binomial nomenclature;
assess the importance of standardising binomial nomenclature in scientific communication and research across different disciplines;

define the basic terms related to phylogenetic trees:
a. common ancestor,
b. clade,
c. monophyletic group,
d. paraphyletic group,
e. polyphyletic group;
identify the key components of a phylogenetic tree, i.e., nodes, branches, clades and common ancestors;
differentiate between monophyletic, paraphyletic and polyphyletic groups within phylogenetic trees;
analyse phylogenetic trees to reveal the evolutionary relationships between organisms;
describe the discovery of viruses;
describe the structural features of viruses;
describe the survival of viruses inside a host cell;
classify viruses based on their structure, type of nucleic acid and host;
list diseases caused by viruses in animals and plants;
describe the structure of a bacteriophage and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV);
illustrate lytic and lysogenic life cycles of bacteriophage;
illustrate different stages of HIV life cycle;
justify the name of the virus, i.e., ‘Human Immunodeficiency Virus’ by establishing linkage with T-helper cells as the basis of immune system;

describe causative agent, symptoms, treatment, preventive measures and source of transmission of the following viral diseases:
a. hepatitis,
b. polio,
c. herpes,
d. acquired immunedeficiency syndrome (AIDS),
e. leaf curl disease of cotton;
define antivirals and antiretroviral drugs;
differentiate between prions and viroids;
list diseases caused by prions and viroids;
evaluate the potential risks posed by prions and viroids to public health and agriculture, considering factors such as transmissibility, environmental persistence and host susceptibility.
state the characteristic features of prokaryotes;
state the discovery, occurrence and habitat of bacteria;

describe the unique features of the following types of archaebacteria:
a. methanogens,
b. halophiles,
c. thermophiles;
describe morphological diversity (shapes) of bacteria;
differentiate between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria with reference to their colour and composition of cell wall;

relate the structure of each component of bacterial cell with its function:
a. glycocalyx,
b. capsule and slime,
c. cell wall,
d. cell membrane,
e. cytoplasmic matrix,
f. mesosomes,
g. chromatin,
h. nucleoid,
i. plasmid,
j. endospore,
k. ribosomes,
l. flagella,
m. pili;
compare prokaryotes with eukaryotes;

differentiate between archaebacteria and eubacteria in the following aspects:
a. habitat,
b. cell wall composition,
c. membrane lipids,
d. genetic material,
e. sensitivity to antibiotics;
analyse the effect of specific cellular components, i.e., cell wall and flagella, on the survival and reproduction of bacteria in various environmental conditions;
compare the chlorophyll present in bacteria and plants;
describe obligatory aerobes, micro-aerobes, facultative and obligatory anaerobes with examples;

compare chemotaxis and magnetotaxis methods of locomotion in bacteria in the following aspects:
a. stimulus for locomotion,
b. key locomotory structures,
c. direction of movement,
d. purpose;
illustrate the different phases of growth in bacteria;
describe endospore formation in bacteria as a mechanism of survival to withstand unfavourable conditions;

explain the economic importance of bacteria in:
a. medicine,
b. agriculture,
c. industry,
d. symbiosis,
e. research and technology;

describe the following physical methods to disrupt bacterial structures or metabolic processes by inhibiting growth or killing bacteria:
a. heat (e.g., autoclaving, pasteurisation),
b. filtration,
c. irradiation (e.g., use of UV light);

describe the action of following chemical agents to prevent growth or kill bacteria:
a. disinfectants (e.g., chlorine, alcohol),
b. antiseptics (e.g., iodine, hydrogen peroxide),
c. antibiotics (e.g., bactericidal and bacteriostatic);
evaluate the consequences of misuse of antibiotics, including antimicrobial resistance of antibiotics;
describe the symptoms, causative agent, treatments and preventive measures of bacterial diseases in man, i.e., cholera, typhoid, tuberculosis and pneumonia;
describe the symptoms, causative bacteria and preventive measures of bacterial diseases in plants, i.e., spots, blights, soft rots, wilts and galls;
list general characteristics of cyanobacteria;
describe the habitat, structure, nutrition and reproduction in Nostoc;

describe the ecological role of cyanobacteria [(e.g., contribution to primary production, nutrient cycling (especially nitrogen fixation), oxygen production and symbiotic relationships)] in aquatic ecosystems.
describe the general characteristics of protists;
describe the evolution of diversity among protists;
justify protists as a polyphyletic group of organisms;
describe the salient features of different classes of animal-like protists, i.e., flagellates/ zooflagellates, sarcodina/ rhizopoda, ciliata/ ciliophora, suctoria and sporozoa/ apicomplexan;
describe the importance of animal-like protist with reference to their ecological roles, i.e., in nutrient cycling, predation on bacteria and other protists and as food sources for larger organisms;

describe the common pathogenic animal-like protists (e.g., entamoeba, plasmodium, trypanosoma and giardia) and the diseases caused by them (e.g., amoebic dysentery, malaria, African sleeping sickness and giardiasis);
compare the salient features of plant-like protists, i.e., euglenoids, dinoflagellates, diatoms, brown, red and green algae with examples;

describe the importance of plant-like protists in food webs as primary producers and impact of algal blooms on aquatic ecosystem and in food industries such as (e.g., algal products, biofuel production);
describe the salient features of fungi-like protists with examples;
describe the life cycle of slime molds (myxomycota) and water molds (oomycota);
describe the contribution of fungi-like protists in the decomposition of organic material and nutrient cycling in ecosystems;
justify the classification of animal-like protists, plant-like protists and fungi-like protists by comparing them with animals, plants and fungi respectively;
describe plant diseases caused by fungi-like protists, i.e., potato blight (caused by Phytophthora infestans) and their impact on agriculture and food security.
compare the cellular features of fungi, animals and plants;
describe the basic structures of fungi, i.e., hyphae, mycelium, spores and fruiting bodies;
describe the structure of hyphae, i.e., septate and coenocytic hyphae along with their role in nutrient absorption and growth;
identify the unique components of fungal cell walls, i.e., chitin and glucans along with their role in providing structural support and protection;
explain mutualistic relationships in fungi, i.e., lichens and mycorrhizae (ectomycorrhiza and endomycorrhiza);
describe different methods of asexual reproduction in fungi, i.e., spores, conidia, fragmentation and budding;
describe different steps of sexual reproduction in fungi, i.e., plasmogamy, karyogamy, meiosis and spore formation;
classify kingdom fungi on the basis of their sexual reproductive structures (zygomycota, ascomycota, basidiomycota and deuteromycota);
describe the life cycle of Rhizopus, focusing on the formation of zygospores during sexual reproduction and sporangia during asexual reproduction;
describe the life cycle of a typical ascomycete, emphasising the formation of ascospores within asci during sexual reproduction and conidia during asexual reproduction;
describe the life cycle of a basidiomycete, highlighting the formation of basidiospores on basidia during sexual reproduction;
define parasexuality in deuteromycetes;
describe the main stages of parasexual life cycle of deuteromycetes, i.e., plasmogamy, karyogamy and mitotic recombination;
describe that genetic recombination occurs without meiosis during parasexual life cycle;
explain ecological and commercial importance of fungi (e.g., economic gains and losses).
state general characteristics of plants;
classify kingdom plantae;
describe the salient features of bryophytes (non-vascular plants) along with their sub-divisions, i.e., musci, hepaticae and anthocerotae;
illustrate the life cycle of moss (polytrichum);
describe the significance of alternation of generation in bryophytes;
explain the adaptive characteristics of bryophytes in the land habitat;
state characteristic features of tracheophytes;

compare the characteristic features of major groups of tracheophyta, i.e.:
a. psilopsida,
b. lycopsida,
c. sphenopsida,
d. pteropsida;
explain evolution of single-veined (microphyllus) and multi- veined (megaphyllus) leaf;
differentiate between homospory and heterospory;
explain the evolution of seed;
illustrate the life cycle of ferns;
describe general characteristics of gymnosperms and angiosperms with examples;
describe the development of male and female gametophytes in angiosperms and gymnosperms;
illustrate the life cycles of gymnosperm and angiosperm plants;
compare the features of dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous plants;
analyse specific adaptations in vascular plants that make them successful land plants, i.e., root systems, lignified cell walls, cuticle layer, xylem, phloem and seed production;

explain the inflorescence**, floral characteristics and economic importance of the following angiospermic families: (Note: **Only Racemose and cymose inflorescence, further description of sub types is not required.)
a. Brassicacaeae,
b. Solanaceae,
c. Poaceae;
derive the floral formulae and floral diagrams of the flowers of angiospermic families (given in SLO 8.5.1).
describe the general characteristics of animals;

explain the body plan of various phyla of kingdom animalia based on the following aspects:
a. type of symmetry (radial and bilateral symmetry),
b. tissue organisation (diploblastic and triploblastic),
c. body cavities (acoelomates, pseudocoelomates and coelomates),
d. pattern of development (protostomes and deuterostomes);

c. radial symmetry,
d. polymorphism and alternation of generation,
e. formation of coral reefs,
f. economic importance;
explain the general characteristics, parasitic adaptations and economic importance of platyhelminthes;
explain the general characteristics, parasitic adaptations and economic importance of nematodes;

explain general characteristics of annelids with reference to their:
a. general characteristics,
b. segmentation and its advantages,
c. coelom and its advantages
d. economic importance;
explain the general characteristics of arthropods and insects;

explain the key adaptations in insects that enable them to survive in diverse habitats;

explain the general characteristics and economic importance of molluscs;
explain the general characteristics of spiny skinned animals (echinoderms) and their affinities;
compare the characteristics of different invertebrate phyla;
describe the fundamental characteristics of chordates;
classify chordates with examples;
describe the general characteristics of super-class pisces;
differentiate among cyclostomes, chondrichthyes (cartilaginous) and osteichthyes (bony fishes) with examples;
describe aquatic adaptations of super-class pisces;
list some familiar edible fish in Pakistan;
describe the general characteristics of amphibians with examples;
elaborate that amphibians are unsuccessful land vertebrates;
explain general characteristics of reptiles;
elaborate reptiles as successful land vertebrates;
describe general characteristics of birds;
explain the adaptations of birds for aerial mode of life (flight adaptations);
differentiate between running and flying birds;
describe general characteristics and classification of mammals (e.g., prototheria, metatheria and eutheria);
compare prototheria, metatheria and eutheria based on their reproductive strategies, anatomical features, geographic distribution and examples;
compare the characteristics of various classes of vertebrates, i.e., fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
define bioenergetics;
describe the structure of ATP and its mechanism of storing energy in high-energy phosphate bonds;
define photosynthesis with word and chemical equation;
describe the significance of photosynthesis;
illustrate the internal structure of thylakoid membrane to show the arrangement of photosynthetic pigments in the form of photosystems, electron transport chain and ATP-synthase complex;
explain the role of chlorophyll and other photosynthetic pigments, light, carbon dioxide and water in photosynthesis;
illustrate the absorption spectrum and action spectrum of photosynthetic pigments (e.g., chlorophyll a, b and carotenoids);
illustrate the main events of light dependent reactions (energy conversion, formation of ATP and NADPH) through Z-scheme;
compare cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation in light dependent reactions;
illustrate the different phases of Calvin cycle/ light independent reactions/ dark reactions, i.e., carbon fixation, reduction and regeneration;
summarise the products formed at each step of light dependent and light independent reactions by detailing the specific molecules produced and their quantities;
explain the process and importance of photorespiration;
describe the effect of temperature on the oxidative activity of RuBP carboxylase;
compare C3, C4 (Hatch-Stack pathway) and CAM plants;

define the following terms:
a. cellular respiration,
b. substrate level phosphorylation,
c. oxidative phosphorylation and chemiosmosis;
differentiate between alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation;

relate the structure of the mitochondrion, [including the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae, ATP synthase and electron transport chain complexes), intermembrane space, matrix and outer membrane] to their roles in ATP production during the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis;

analyse the steps involved in the mechanism of cellular respiration:
a. glycolysis,
b. pyruvic acid oxidation/ link reaction (formation of acetyl CoA),
c. Krebs cycle (Citric acid cycle),
d. respiratory chain (oxidative phosphorylation);
explain the substrate-level phosphorylation during which exergonic reactions coupled with the synthesis of ATP, i.e., glycolysis and Krebs cycle;
relate chemiosmosis with electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation;

summarise the products formed at each step of cellular respiration, i.e., glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation by detailing the specific molecules produced and their quantities;
describe the formation of acetyl CoA from fats through β oxidation;
compare the cellular respiration of fats and glucose.
define nutrition;
list the macro and micronutrients of plants;

describe the role and deficiency symptoms of:
a. nitrogen,
b. phosphorus,
c. potassium,
d. magnesium;
assess leaf colour and growth patterns of various plants to diagnose specific nutrient deficiencies;
explain different modes of heterotrophic nutrition in plants, i.e., saprophytic, parasitic, symbiotic and insectivorous;

relate the structure of each organ of human digestive system with its function:
a. gastrointestinal tract (GIT):
i. oral cavity, ii. pharynx, iii. oesophagus, iv. stomach,
v. small intestine, vi. large intestine, vii. rectum and anus,
b. accessory digestive organs:
i. tongue, ii. salivary glands (composition of saliva), iii. liver (composition of bile), iv. gall bladder,
v. pancreas (composition of pancreatic juice);
describe the structure and function of different types of human teeth, i.e., incisors, canines, premolars and molars;
analyse the human dental formula (2-1-2-3) for both primary and permanent dentition;

relate each structural component of a human tooth, i.e., crown, root, enamel, dentin, pulp cavity, cementum, periodontal ligament and gingiva with its function in processes like chewing, protection and sensory response;
describe factors that contribute to dental health issues, i.e., poor oral hygiene, dietary habits, smoking or tobacco use, lack of regular dental care and genetic predisposition;
describe the characteristics and preventive measures of common dental diseases, i.e., dental caries, gingivitis, periodontitis, halitosis (bad breath), tooth sensitivity;
evaluate dietary choices that affects the human dentition and overall oral health;
describe three stages of swallowing: the oral (voluntary), pharyngeal (involuntary) and oesophageal (involuntary) phases;
describe the coordination of circular and longitudinal muscles in peristalsis;
explain the processes of mechanical and chemical digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids in different parts of human digestive system;
describe the role of gastrin, secretin and cholecystokinin (CCK) hormones in stimulating secretion of digestive enzymes and production of gastric acid;

analyse the following:
a. impact of gastric glands malfunction on acid and enzyme secretion,
b. symptoms of acid reflux in relation to the malfunction of lower oesophageal sphincter/ cardiac sphincter,
c. role of the pyloric sphincter in regulating food passage,
d. consequences of damage to the mucosal lining in terms of protection against acidic content;
compare the mechanisms of absorption of nutrients, i.e., amino acids, monosaccharides and fatty acids by small intestine;
explain the role of the lymphatic system in lipid absorption;
evaluate the consequences of structural damage to the small intestine on nutrient absorption, i.e., loss of any structural component of villi;
identify the regions of the large intestine, i.e., caecum, appendix, ascending colon, transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and anus;

describe the structural features of the large intestine, including its thick muscular walls that facilitate movement of waste and the presence of goblet cells that secrete mucus to aid in lubrication;

assess the role of the large intestine in the absorption of water and electrolytes, formation and storage of faeces and role of gut microbiota in synthesising essential vitamins like vitamin K and certain B vitamins;

describe causes, symptoms, treatment and preventive measures of gastrointestinal disorders, i.e., diarrhoea, dysentery, constipation, piles, dyspepsia, peptic ulcer, food poisoning, anorexia and bulimia nervosa.
describe gaseous exchange in plants through stomata, lenticels and the leaf surface;

relate the structure of each respiratory organ with its function:
a. upper respiratory tract:
i. nose (nasal cavity), ii. pharynx, iii. larynx,
b. lower respiratory tract:
i. trachea, ii. bronchi and bronchioles, iii. chest cavity, ribs, external and internal intercostal muscles, diaphragm, iii. lungs, iv. pleurae;

explain structural adaptations in alveoli that collectively optimise the efficiency of gaseous exchange, i.e., large surface area, single layer of epithelial cells, rich capillary network, thin layer of moisture, surfactant and presence of macrophages;
explain the mechanism of breathing, i.e., inspiration and expiration;

describe the neural and physiological mechanisms involved in the involuntary control of breathing, i.e., the roles of medulla oblongata, pons and peripheral chemoreceptors (e.g., carotid bodies and aortic bodies);
explain the transportation of carbon dioxide and oxygen by the blood;
relate the structures of haemoglobin and myoglobin with their function as respiratory pigments;

evaluate the impact of environmental factors on the efficiency of breathing mechanisms and respiratory system, i.e., high altitude, air pollution and smoking;

explain causes, symptoms and preventive measures of:
a. upper respiratory tract infections:
i. sinusitis, ii. otitis media,
b. lower respiratory tract infections:
i. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease or COPD (chronic bronchitis, emphysema and asthma), ii. lung cancer.
describe the importance of transport of materials in living organisms;
define water potential, osmotic/ solute potential and pressure potential;
differentiate between plasmolysis and deplasmolysis;
analyse the effects of different solute concentrations on plant and animal cells;
calculate water potentials of plant cells;
explain apoplast, symplast and vacuolar pathways through which water and minerals can move into the root system;
relate the structure of xylem and phloem to their functions;
explain that ascent of sap in plants is driven by TACT mechanism (Transpiration pull, Adhesion, Cohesion, Tension), root pressure, capillary action and imbibition;
define transpiration;
differentiate among cuticular, lenticular and stomatal transpiration;

assess the effect of following factors on the rate of transpiration:
a. light,
b. wind,
c. humidity,
d. temperature;
explain transpiration as a necessary evil;
define translocation;
exemplify different parts of plants that function as sources or sinks in relation to the movement of nutrients;
explain the mechanism of phloem translocation, i.e., diffusion and pressure flow hypothesis;

slos.description:

e. layers of heart wall,
a. chambers,
b. valves and associated blood vessels;
explain the sequence of events in the cardiac cycle, including the contraction and relaxation of atria and ventricles;
describe the functioning of heart valves (tricuspid, bicuspid, pulmonary and aortic valves) in maintaining unidirectional blood flow during the cardiac cycle and producing heart sounds (lub-dub);
analyse the pressure changes in the left side of the heart during a cardiac cycle;
define the terms: cardiac output, heart/ pulse rate and stroke volume;
calculate cardiac output by using the formula (Cardiac Output = Heart Rate × Stroke Volume) during rest, exercise and stress;
assess that different bodily states affect the cardiac output, i.e., resting, physical exercise or stress;

explain the following:
a. role of the sinoatrial (SA) node as the natural pacemaker,
b. transmission of electrical impulses through the atrioventricular (AV) node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres,
c. sequence of electrical conduction in coordinating the contraction of atria and ventricles;
describe the function of an artificial pacemaker in regulating heart rhythm in cases of sinoatrial (SA) node dysfunction or conduction blockages;
analyse different components of ECG report, i.e., ECG waveform (P wave, QRS complex, T wave) and their relationship to cardiac cycles and electrical activity;
explain the causes of blue babies with reference to atrial and ventricular septum defects and ductus arteriosus;
explain the structure, function and composition of each blood component, i.e., plasma and blood cells;
describe the functions of blood;

describe the causes, symptoms, preventions and treatments of disorders of blood, i.e.:
a. leukaemia,
b. thalassemia,
c. anaemia,
d. haemophilia;
relate the structure of artery, vein and capillary with their functions;
describe the role of precapillary sphincters in regulating the flow of blood through capillaries;
trace the pathway of blood through the pulmonary and systemic circulation, i.e., coronary, hepatic-portal and renal circulation;
analyse the factors, i.e., vessel diameter and total cross-sectional area, affecting the rate of blood flow and blood pressure through arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules and veins;
differentiate between blood pressure and pulse pressure;
interpret normal and abnormal pulse pressure values and their potential health implications;
describe the role of baroreceptors and volume receptors in regulating the blood pressure;
describe various aspects of cardiovascular health, i.e., atherosclerosis, arteriosclerosis, thrombus formation, embolus, coronary thrombosis, stroke, haemorrhage and hypertension;
categorise angina pectoris, heart attack and heart failure as progressive stages in the development of cardiovascular disease;

describe the purpose of angiography, including its role in visualising blood vessels and diagnosing conditions such as blockages or aneurysms (localised, abnormal dilation or bulging of a blood vessel due to a weakened vessel wall);
describe the basic procedure of angiography, including the use of contrast dye and imaging techniques to obtain detailed pictures of blood vessels;
describe the main principles of angioplasty and open-heart surgery (coronary bypass);
describe the causes of hypertension and hypotension;

design a lifestyle modification plan that includes dietary changes, physical activity, stress management and smoking cessation strategies tailored to individuals at risk of or suffering from hypertension or cardiovascular diseases;

explain the lymphatic system with respect to:
a. formation of lymph,
b. lymph vessels,
c. lymph trunk,
d. lymph nodes,
e. lymphoid organs/ masses/ tissues (e.g., bone marrow, thymus, adenoids, tonsils, spleen, Peyer’s patches and appendix);
compare intercellular fluid (tissue fluid) and lymph;
explain the functions of lymphatic system;
assess that malfunctioning of lymphatic system leads to oedema.

subtopics.name: 14.1 Introduction and Types of Immune System

slos.description: define immunity;
classify immune system as innate [first (non-specific) and second line of defense)] and adaptive [(specific) antibody-mediated and cell-mediated as third line of defense)] immune systems;

explain the role of physical barriers (e.g., skin, ciliated epithelium, nasal hairs and mucous membrane) and chemical barriers (e.g., stomach acid, tears, mucus, saliva) in protecting the body from infection as the first line of defense;
describe the structure and mode of action of phagocytes, i.e., neutrophils, macrophages, natural killer cells and antigen-presenting cells;
identify the roles of cytokines, opsonin, phagosomes and lysosomes in immune response;
explain the non-specific responses of the body to infection, including inflammation, lysozyme action, interferon and phagocytosis;
compare the bacterial-killing function of complement system proteins and the virus-inhibiting role of interferons;
describe the release of pyrogens by microbes and their effect on the hypothalamus to boost the body’s temperature;
describe the structural features of an antibody, i.e., variable and constant regions, heavy and light chains and antigen-binding sites;
describe the role of B-cells in recognising antigens, producing antibodies and retaining memory for the long-term immunity;
explain the process of clonal selection and expansion of B-cells in response to an antigen;
describe that antibodies neutralise pathogens, opsonise them for phagocytosis and activate the complement system;
describe the role of T-cells in recognising and responding to infected or abnormal cells;
identify the different types of T-cells (helper T-cells, cytotoxic or killer T-cells and regulatory or suppressor T-cells) and their specific functions in the immune response;
describe that cytotoxic T-cells destroy infected or cancerous cells by releasing perforins and granzymes;
explain the process of T-cell activation, including the roles of antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules;
explain the role of helper T-cells in supporting the activation and function of other immune cells, including B-cells and macrophages;
state the role of T-cells and B-cells in transplant rejections;
describe the primary immune response, including the lag phase, production of antibodies and gradual increase in antibody concentration;
explain the secondary immune response, highlighting the faster and more robust production of antibodies, due to the presence of memory B cells;
illustrate the differences between primary and secondary immune responses in terms of antibody concentration and response time;

subtopics.name: 14.6 Active and Passive Immunity (Natural and Artificial)

slos.description: differentiate between active (natural and artificial) and passive (natural and artificial) immunity;

identify immunisation strategies for active immunity (e.g., first exposure to a pathogen, vaccination) and passive immunity (e.g., administration of antibodies through antiserum or immunoglobulin injections and the natural transfer of antibodies from mother to infant through breastfeeding or placental transfer);

evaluate real-life scenarios to decide whether a patient should receive active or passive immunity or both immunities, i.e., exposure to rabies, snakebite, tetanus wound, hepatitis B virus, newborn protection, measles in an unvaccinated individual and immune deficiency disorder);
describe the role of histamines in producing allergy symptoms in humans;
define autoimmune diseases;
exemplify autoimmune diseases, i.e., rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, multiple sclerosis and type-1 diabetes;
define monoclonal antibodies;
describe the steps of production of monoclonal antibodies through hybridoma method, i.e., immunisation, cell fusion, selection and cloning, production and purification);

describe the applications of monoclonal antibodies in the following:
a. disease treatment, i.e., cancer, autoimmune disorders and infectious diseases,
b. diagnostic tests, i.e., pregnancy tests, blood tests and viral infection tests.

slos.description: define homeostasis;
differentiate among the different aspects of homeostasis, i.e., osmoregulation, excretion and thermoregulation;
describe the significance of homeostasis with examples;
describe the components of the feedback system in living organisms, i.e., stimulus, receptor/ detector, control centre, effector and response/ output with examples;
explain positive feedback systems in humans with examples, i.e., blood clotting, childbirth/ labour contractions, lactation/ milk ejection reflex;
explain negative feedback systems in humans with examples, i.e., blood glucose regulation;

explain osmoregulatory adaptations in plants, i.e.:
a. hydrophytes,
b. halophytes,
c. mesophytes,
d. xerophytes;
differentiate between osmoregulator and osmoconformer animals with examples;
explain osmoregulatory adaptations in aquatic (fresh water and marine fish) and terrestrial animals;
differentiate between excretion, egestion and secretion;
explain different ways in which excretory products are stored and removed from plant body;
differentiate between transpiration and guttation as methods of removal of water in plants;
analyse the relationship between the mode of nitrogenous excretion and the habitat of animals, i.e., ammoniotelic, uricotelic and ureotelic;
identify different excretory organs in man, i.e., kidney, liver, skin, with the type of metabolic waste excreted by each of them;
explain the steps of the urea cycle or ornithine cycle;
explain the role of liver in homeostasis;
identify the function of each part of the urinary system;
describe the shape, location and protective coverings of the kidney (fibrous capsule);
describe the internal structure of kidney, i.e., cortex, medulla, renal pyramids, renal pelvis, calyces and nephrons;
relate the internal structure of nephron with its functions (simple filtration, reabsorption and secretion);
identify glomerular capillaries and peritubular capillaries as two major capillary beds in kidneys;
explain the effect of hormones, i.e., antidiuretic hormone, aldosterone and parathyroid hormone on the working of kidneys;
analyse the effects of changes in antidiuretic hormone levels on urine concentration and the body’s hydration status under conditions such as dehydration or excessive water intake;
state the composition of urine in a healthy person;
interpret urine test results (for presence of proteins, glucose, blood, or altered electrolyte levels) to identify dysfunctions of specific part of nephron;
describe the causative bacteria and symptoms of urinary tract infections, i.e., pyelonephritis, urethritis and cystitis;
explain the causes and treatments of kidney stones;
describe the causes and treatments of kidney failure;
explain the mechanism and problems related to dialysis, i.e., haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis;
describe the principles of kidney transplant with respect to blood compatibility;
identify the problems associated with administration of immunosuppressant drugs after kidney transplant;
describe the significance of thermoregulation in living organisms;
describe adaptations of plants to low and high temperatures;

subtopics.name: 15.9 Thermoregulation in Animals mative Assessment, not to be assessed under

slos.description: classify animals on the basis of their ability to thermoregulate, i.e., poikilotherms and homeotherms with examples;
compare the mechanisms of ectothermy, heterothermy and endothermy with examples;
analyse structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations in animals for thermoregulation in different environments.
describe the role of turgor pressure in providing support to herbaceous plants;

differentiate among different supporting structures in plants, i.e., parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma (fibres/ tracheids, vessels, sclereids and stone cells) in terms of their structure, function, location and examples;
differentiate between primary and secondary growth in plants;
explain the significance of secondary growth in plants;
describe the formation and significance of annual rings;
explain types of tropic movements, i.e., phototropism, geotropism, thigmotropism, hydrotropism, chemotropism and thermotropism with examples;
explain types of nastic movements, i.e., nyctinastic (sleeping), photonastic, thermonastic, thigmonastic (haptonastic) and seismonastic movements with examples;
discuss that hormones like auxins control tropisms (phototropism and geotropism) by distributing hormones unevenly to stimulate directional growth;
define skeleton;
compare hydrostatic skeleton, exoskeleton and endoskeleton with respect to their structure, composition, location, flexibility, growth, protection, adaptation for movement and examples;
explain the composition and structure of compact and spongy bone;
compare bone and cartilage based on their composition, hardness, function, blood supply, strength and regenerative ability;
compare the hyaline cartilage, fibrocartilage and elastic cartilage based on their flexibility, composition and location;
explain the structure, function and articulation of different components of human skeletal system, i.e., axial and appendicular skeleton;
explain the functions of human skeleton;
explain different types of joints, i.e., immovable/ fixed, slightly movable/ cartilaginous, freely movable/ synovial joints (with their sub-types);
elaborate the structure of a synovial joint;
compare tendon and ligament in terms of their composition, function, elasticity, location and role in movement;
differentiate between origin and insertion as attachment points of muscles on bones with examples, i.e., biceps brachii;
evaluate the impact of improper joint alignment (dislocation) on mobility and the potential for long-term damage to the skeletal system;

explain the causes, symptoms, treatments and preventive measures of skeleton-related diseases, i.e.:
a. disc slip (herniated disc),
b. spondylitis,
c. sciatica,
d. osteoarthritis,
e. osteoporosis;
analyse clinical cases of skeleton-related diseases, based on the symptoms or diagnostic tests, i.e., X-rays, MRIs;
suggest appropriate management strategies for skeleton-related diseases given in SLO 16.5.1;
explain the process of repairing of fractured bones;
recommend modifications to the workplace to prevent strain on the axial and appendicular skeletons;
differentiate between voluntary and involuntary muscles;
relate the structure of different types of muscles with their functions, i.e., skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscles;
describe the ultrastructure of skeletal muscles;
illustrate the changes in the sarcomere during contraction and relaxation;
explain the mechanism of muscle contraction (sliding filament theory of Huxley, cross bridge cycle and regulation of muscle contraction);

describe the cause and mechanism of rigor mortis (including the depletion of ATP, calcium ion accumulation and the formation of sustained cross-bridges between actin and myosin in muscle fibres) after death;
predict the effects of calcium deficiency and ATP depletion on muscle contraction;
describe all or none response in muscles;
compare the structure and functions of fast twitch and slow twitch muscle fibres;
describe the causes of abnormal muscle contraction, i.e., tetany and cramps;
define antagonistic muscles;
describe the action of antagonistic muscles, i.e., quadriceps and hamstrings in the movement of knee joint;
differentiate between tetanus and muscle tetany.
define coordination and control in living organisms;
describe the need for coordination and control;
explain the types of plant hormones with their functions;
describe that plants respond to stress factors, i.e., drought, temperature changes and salinity, through hormones like abscisic acid, which can promote stomatal closure to reduce water loss;
describe commercial applications of plant hormones;
define biological clock and circadian rhythm;

identify different physiological processes influenced by circadian rhythms, i.e., sleep-wake cycles, hormone secretion (e.g., cortisol in the morning and melatonin at night), flowering time and leaf movements;
define nervous coordination, receptors and neurons;
classify receptors based on the types of stimuli;
describe the working of sensory mechanoreceptors with reference to skin, i.e., Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner corpuscles, Merkel complexes, Ruffini corpuscles;
compare the structure and function of sensory, relay/ intermediate and motor neurons;
describe the role of neuroglial cells in the nervous system (e.g., Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes);
classify neurons based on their structural differences, i.e., multipolar, unipolar, bipolar and pseudo-unipolar;
differentiate between myelinated and non-myelinated neurons;
define nerve impulse;
describe the factors affecting the velocities of nerve impulse, i.e., temperature, diameter of axon, myelination in neurons;
analyse different steps involved in the action potential and propagation of nerve impulse;
describe saltatory conduction of nerve impulse in a myelinated neuron;
define synapse, pre synapse, post synapse and neurotransmitter;
explain synaptic transmission of nerve impulse;
classify neurotransmitters as inhibitory (e.g., Gamma- aminobutyric acid (GABA), glycine and serotonin) and excitatory (e.g., glutamate, epinephrine and norepinephrine);

explain the functions of different parts of human brain;
analyse the impact of injuries to various regions of the brain, i.e., the cerebrum, cerebellum, brainstem and basal ganglia on motor coordination such as movement, balance and fine motor skills;
analyse the structures visible in the cross-section of spinal cord;
describe cranial and spinal nerves in man;
describe peripheral nervous system along with its subtypes, i.e., somatic and autonomic nervous systems;
differentiate between sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems;

trace the sequence of events in a reflex arc (from stimulus detection by the receptor, signal transmission along the sensory neuron, processing in the spinal cord and response through the motor neuron to the effector.);
illustrate monosynaptic and polysynaptic reflexes;

subtopics.name: 17.6 Effects of Drugs on Human Nervous System

explain drug addiction and drug tolerance with reference to nicotine and caffeine and their adverse effects on nervous system;
describe that pain medicines can reduce or numb pain in the human body;
describe that certain pain medications are addictive;
describe narcotic drugs as agents that interact with the normal nervous activity;
classify nervous disorders into vascular, infectious, structural, functional and degenerative disorders;

describe the causes, symptoms and treatment of each category of disorders (e.g., stroke as vascular, meningitis as infectious, brain tumor as structural, headache as functional, and Alzheimer disease as degenerative disorder);
describe EEG, CT scan and MRI as important diagnostic tests for nervous disorders with examples;
assess clinical symptoms and diagnostic results to identify various nervous system disorders;
differentiate between nervous and chemical coordination;
identify the major endocrine glands and their locations in the human body, i.e., pituitary, hypothalamus, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pancreas, adrenal, testes and ovaries);
explain the hormones secreted by each endocrine gland and their functions;
describe the neurosecretory role of hypothalamus;
assess the role of hormones and the problems associated with their imbalance in the body;
illustrate the negative feedback mechanism of hormones, i.e., thyroxin and cortisol;
describe positive feedback with reference to oxytocin and negative feedback with reference to insulin and glucagon;

analyse the role of insulin and glucagon in regulation of blood glucose levels through the processes of glycogenesis, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in different scenarios (e.g., after a meal, during fasting, intense physical activity, diabetes mellitus or hypoglycaemia);
describe the chemical nature of hormones;
identify different cell signalling molecules (ligands), i.e., hormones and neurotransmitters;
explain different types of cell surface receptors and intracellular receptors and the process through which they bind to signalling molecules (ligands);
explain signal transduction pathways (for protein and steroid hormones) with the key components like G-proteins, kinases and secondary messengers such as cAMP.
compare asexual reproduction and sexual reproduction in plants;
describe advantages and disadvantages of asexual reproduction;

exemplify natural and artificial methods of reproduction in plants, i.e.,
a. vegetative reproduction,
b. parthenocarpy,
c. apomixes;
define photoperiodism, long day, short day and day neutral plants;
explain the mechanism of photoperiodism with respect to mode of action of phytochromes;
differentiate between florigen and phytochromes;
describe seed dormancy;
differentiate between epigeal, hypogeal and viviparous germination of seeds with examples;
define vernalisation;
explain the effect of low temperature treatment on flower production in biennials and perennials;

compare the following:
a. internal fertilisation and external fertilisation,
b. identical and fraternal twins,
c. spermatogenesis and oogenesis,
d. unisexual and bisexual animals,
e. oviparity, viviparity and ovoviviparity;
describe the male and female reproductive systems of humans;
describe male reproductive hormones and their functions;

explain different stages of female reproductive cycles, i.e., ovarian cycle (follicular phase, ovulation and luteal phases) and uterine cycle (menstrual, proliferative and secretory phases) with their hormonal control in human females;
analyse the effect of hormonal levels on the female reproductive cycles;

describe causative agent, symptoms and prevention of sexually transmitted diseases, i.e.:
a. gonorrhoea,
b. syphilis,
c. genital herpes,
d. acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS).
define open growth, growing points and meristems in plants;
describe the types of meristems with their functions in plants;
describe different phases of growth in plants;
explain external and internal factors affecting the growth rate in plants;
describe cell differentiation in the embryo of a plant;
explain growth correlations and their effects (inhibitory and compensatory) in plants;
describe the key events in development of animals;
differentiate between animal and vegetal pole of avian/ hen egg;
describe the cleavage pattern of avian/ hen egg;
describe development of chick up to three germinal layers;

explain the stages of chick development, i.e.:
a. morula formation,
b. blastulation,
c. gastrulation,
d. notochord formation,
e. neurulation,
f. somites and coelom formation;
explain fate of the three germ layers that form during gastrulation;
explain the role of nucleus and cytoplasm in development through Hans Spemann’s experiments;
explain the role of nucleus in development through experiments performed on Acetabularia;
define cell differentiation;
describe the significance of cell differentiation;

describe the following factors that control cell differentiation and gene expression:
a. cytoplasmic determinants,
b. signalling molecules or induction,
c. transcription factors,
d. DNA methylation,
e. histone modifications,
f. apoptosis,
g. environmental factors, e.g., nutrients, hormones, physical signals;
explain embryonic induction as investigated by Hans Spemann and Hilde Mangold;
define gerontology;
describe aging as a part of normal development;
differentiate between primary and secondary aging in humans;
explain the genetic and extrinsic factors responsible for aging;
define teratology;
describe abnormalities inherited from parent to offspring (at gene level and chromosomal level) with examples;
relate different environmental and metabolic factors with abnormal development.

differentiate among the types of chromosomes, i.e.:
a. autosomes and sex chromosomes,
b. homologous and non-homologous chromosomes,
c. telocentric, acrocentric, metacentric and sub-metacentric chromosomes;
describe levels of eukaryotic chromosomal organisation;
define chromosome karyotype;
describe the significance of chromosome karyotype in genetics;
analyse karyotype images to identify chromosomal abnormalities in humans;
differentiate between heterochromatin and euchromatin;

explain deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) as heredity material with reference to the experiments conducted by:
a. Frederick Griffith,
b. Colin Macleod,
c. Maclyn McCarty,
d. Alfred Hershey,
e. Martha Chase;
assess the double helical molecular structure of DNA;
determine the complementary base composition using Chargaff’s Rule and the impact of changes in base composition (e.g., mutations) on the total hydrogen bond count in a DNA fragment;
illustrate the three proposed models, i.e., conservative, semi conservative and dispersive models of DNA replication;
explain the Meselson and Stahl experiment to demonstrate the semi-conservative replication of DNA;
analyse the process of semi-conservative replication of DNA;
identify DNA stability and variability as two characters of the replicating DNA molecule;
describe mechanisms that contribute to DNA stability, i.e., proofreading during replication, DNA repair systems and structural features of DNA;
describe sources of variability in DNA, i.e., mutations, genetic recombination and genetic drift;
define gene expression;
identify the steps involved in gene expression, including transcription and translation;
describe the importance of regulation of gene expression;
explain the concept of regulatory genes and their role in controlling gene expression;
explain the negative and positive control of gene expression (the lac operon) by repressor and activator proteins respectively;
